title: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
desc: Supports conditional assistance and substantive verification while contrasting certification, prohibition and ordinary-rule approaches.

kps.k: The central proposition is conditional AI assistance without transferring professional or judicial responsibility.
kps.d: Court guidance and ethics opinions generally permit useful AI assistance while preserving duties of competence, candour, confidentiality, supervision and independent judgment. The ABA Task Force argues that existing Model Rules can accommodate responsible use; CCBE and jurisdiction-specific opinions apply their own professional frameworks. These positions do not establish a universal permission: local court orders can impose additional restrictions. The debate concerns how to make continuing human responsibility effective, rather than whether AI authorship excuses defective work.

qs.q: Although the ABA Model Rules were not written to address specific technologies, they are comprehensive enough to permit the responsible and ethical use of generative AI tools in legal practice.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Conclusion  While lawyers’ core professional obligations remain unchanged, the context in which they are applied is rapidly evolving due to technological advancements like GenAI.
qs.a: CCBE Guide on the Use of Generative AI by Lawyers · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification requires substantive human checking, not merely confirming that citations exist.
kps.d: The guidance requires users to assess whether authorities support the attributed propositions, quotations are accurate, law remains current and jurisdictionally applicable, and analysis covers relevant issues and client interests. Ayinde extends responsibility to research supplied by others and to client advice as well as filings. Singapore rejects both AI self-confirmation and cross-tool confirmation as sufficient verification. Victoria’s May 2026 practice note makes an important distinction: users may consult original sources housed within an AI tool. New York and Texas ethics guidance also insist that removing fabrications alone does not establish competent representation.

qs.q: (c)   Verify that any references to case law, legislation, textbooks or articles provided                 as AI-generated content actually exist and stand for the legal positions that are                 attributed to them.
qs.a: Guide on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools by Court Users (Singapore Courts, Registrar's Circular No. 1 of 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: However, Court users may verify GenAI content by referring to original source material housed within a GenAI tool.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Litigation incidents support the case for safeguards, but do not establish a general error rate or prove safeguards effective.
kps.d: Legg, McNamara and Alimardani draw on a dataset of 524 cases identifying litigation use across eight jurisdictions as of 30 September 2025; that count does not mean 524 misuse incidents. Their examples illustrate fabricated authorities, failed supervision and noncompliance with disclosure requirements. Separately, Bell and Rogers report Magesh and colleagues’ 2024 research finding errors across tested legal research products, including retrieval-augmented tools, alongside potential value at the initial research stage. Court warnings, product descriptions, adoption surveys and repeated accounts of the same incidents should not be treated as independent performance evidence or proof of net benefits.

qs.q: As of 30 September 2025,        the dataset comprised 524 cases where GenAI was identified as being used in litigation.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

qs.q: 32 All the products produced incorrect results and hallucinations some of the time, and Magesh et al.
qs.a: Becoming, Doing, Being: GenAI and the Promise of Professional Identity in Law · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Courts differ materially over disclosure, certification and prohibition.
kps.d: Singapore and New Zealand generally require disclosure only when asked; England and Wales makes disclosure of responsible lawyer use context-dependent. Canada’s Federal Court instead requires a first-paragraph declaration for AI co-authorship, excluding manually implemented suggestions and providing a separate route for expert reports. Starr requires certification of non-use or human checking and retains Rule 11 accountability. Browning’s survey contrasts such regimes with Subramanian’s verification-only approach and drafting bans imposed by other judges. Victoria’s May 2026 practice note replaced its May 2024 guidelines and requires readiness to identify AI-produced portions and explain verification, rather than routine disclosure of every use.

qs.q: 5) Disclosing GenAI use You do not need to disclose use of a GenAI chatbot as a matter of course – unless asked by the court or tribunal.
qs.a: Guidelines for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Courts and Tribunals — Lawyers · Regulators & courts · 2023

qs.q: A Declaration is required when the role AI plays in the preparation of materials for the purpose of litigation resembles that of a co-author.
qs.a: Notice to the Parties and the Profession — The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings (amended) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The strongest disagreement concerns whether AI-specific controls improve accountability or impose unnecessary burdens.
kps.d: Canada’s Federal Court justifies common disclosure obligations through fairness between represented and unrepresented parties. Legg and colleagues argue that certification paired with targeted bans makes breaches easier to establish without proving testimony false. Conversely, The Legal Ethics of Generative AI argues that existing filing duties and enforcement powers suffice. Fifth Circuit commenters warn that unclear definitions can capture brainstorming, rejected suggestions or unnoticed embedded features, expose accurate filings to compliance disputes, and stigmatise useful technology. AI, UPL, & A2J predicts restrictions may encourage covert use. These criticisms and deterrence claims are arguments and forecasts, not measured effects of court rules.

qs.q: It would be unfair to place elevated AI-related responsibilities only on these self-represented individuals, and allow counsel to rely on their duties.
qs.a: Notice to the Parties and the Profession — The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Court Proceedings (amended) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: There is no need to establish that the testimony is false.278 As a result, the combination of certifications and bans can aid in the deployment of sanctions.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Evidence preparation attracts stronger restrictions than administrative assistance or legal argument.
kps.d: NSW’s January 2025 SC Gen 23 permits specified preparatory and submission work but prohibits generating or rephrasing witness evidence, requires non-use disclosure, and generally requires prior leave for AI-assisted expert-report content. It preserves preparatory assistance and limited annexure or exhibit exceptions. Singapore permits a compliant first draft of an affidavit or statement while prohibiting evidence fabrication or manipulation. Victoria requires caution and preservation of the witness’s own knowledge and words. These are substantive differences in permissible drafting, despite a shared concern for evidentiary integrity. Expert instructions, leave applications and records therefore need court-specific treatment.

qs.q: Gen AI must not be used for the purpose of altering, embellishing, strengthening     or diluting or otherwise rephrasing a witness’s evidence when expressed in     written form.
qs.a: Supreme Court of NSW Practice Note SC Gen 23 — Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (issued 28 January 2025) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Asking a Generative AI tool to generate a first-cut draft                 of an affidavit/statement can be done (provided that this Guide is complied                 with), but it is not acceptable to ask a Generative AI to fabricate or tamper with                 evidence.
qs.a: Guide on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools by Court Users (Singapore Courts, Registrar's Circular No. 1 of 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Judicial assistance must remain distinct from delegating adjudication, with procedural fairness extending beyond accuracy.
kps.d: The Canadian Judicial Council prohibits delegating decision-making authority regardless of a system’s capabilities. Hong Kong similarly reserves decisions to judges; England and Wales requires judges to read underlying documents rather than substitute AI summaries for direct engagement. Sedona recommendations reproduced in the Year 2 report also warn against automation bias and extrajudicial material parties cannot rebut. Disclosure remains contested: England and Wales generally does not require judges to describe preparation, while Guidelines for the Use of AI Systems in Courts and Tribunals calls for disclosure of AI-assisted drafting. Canada’s Federal Court conditions its own AI decision-making on prior public consultation, not an unconditional ban.

qs.q: It must be unequivocally understood that no judge is permitted to delegate decision-making authority, whether to a law clerk, administrative assistant, or computer program, regardless of their capabilities.
qs.a: Guidelines for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Canadian Courts (Canadian Judicial Council, First Edition, September 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: This includes recognizing that when judicial officers obtain information, analysis, or advice from AI or GenAI tools, they risk relying on extrajudicial information and influences that the parties have not had an opportunity to address or rebut.
qs.a: Addressing the Legal Challenges of AI: Year 2 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Confidentiality and security depend on actual data handling, not a tool’s public, private or specialised label.
kps.d: Guidance calls for scrutiny of retention, training reuse, third-party access, contractual protections and access controls. NSW permits protected litigation inputs only under specified controlled-environment and reuse safeguards. New York’s court-system policy goes further by barring uploads of even public court documents to models outside its defined private environment. Victoria requires scrutiny of closed tools too. Florida and New York ethics opinions distinguish disclosure of confidential information from AI use that discloses none; consent is not universally required for every use. Deepfakes, concealed instructions and AI-enabled fraud add authenticity and cybersecurity risks that citation checks alone cannot address.

qs.q: No user may upload into any generative AI program that does not operate on a private model      any document that has been filed or submitted for filing in any court, even if the document is      classified as public.
qs.a: Interim Policy on the Use of Artificial Intelligence (New York State Unified Court System) · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: 6.9 For closed AI tools:  (a) If Court users input private, confidential or sensitive information into closed AI tools they need to exercise caution and satisfy themselves by reviewing the contractual terms or privacy and confidentiality settings that the information they input will be kept within a secure environment.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Effective governance requires organisational supervision and practical competence, not warnings alone.
kps.d: Legg and colleagues distinguish literacy deficits from verification drift: users may know the risks yet abandon checks under persuasive output and resource pressure. They recommend complementary education, certification, calibrated sanctions and selective prohibition. Ayinde places responsibility on managing partners, heads of chambers and regulators and anticipates scrutiny of leadership compliance. Professional guidance translates this into approved-tool policies, staff training, review procedures and traceable records. California’s 2026 guidance extends the approach to agentic systems, forbidding autonomous court filings or representations without lawyer review and approval. Sanctions remain conduct-specific; negligence, deception and intentional interference should not be conflated.

qs.q: Alternatively, as explained by verification drift, the risks are known but the persuasiveness of GenAI outputs when combined with time and resource pressures leads to risk management steps being foregone.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In those circumstances, practical and effective measures must now be taken by those            within the legal profession with individual leadership responsibilities (such as heads of            chambers and managing partners) and by those with the responsibility for regulating            the provision of legal services.
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Verification creates an unresolved tension between promised efficiency and the cost of responsible use.
kps.d: The Verification-Value Paradox challenges confidence that lawyers can readily manage AI risks, while adoption-oriented guidance presents task-level assistance as a route to better service. The Australian joint statement explicitly warns that verification and correction can unnecessarily increase client costs above traditional methods. New York and California guidance permits charging actual prompting, review and editing time but rejects billing hypothetical hours AI eliminated. The practical implication is to assess the complete workflow, including checking and correction, rather than equate faster generation with cheaper competent work. The supplied material does not quantify net savings or establish a current general duty to adopt AI.

qs.q: However, the increasing number of cases where judges have criticised lawyers for filing hallucinated AI-generated material with courts calls this paradigm into question.
qs.a: The Verification-Value Paradox: A Normative Critique of Gen AI Use in Legal Practice · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Lawyers who use AI should ensure that it does         not unnecessarily increase costs for their client above traditional methods (e.g.
qs.a: Statement on the use of artificial intelligence in Australian legal practice · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Access-to-justice applications expose the limits of safeguards built around expert review.
kps.d: The small-value consumer-claims article argues that conversational tools could help people whose claims cannot justify representation costs, but expressly distinguishes consumer-facing deployment from expert-supervised practice. Judicial guidance recognises that chatbots may provide some litigants’ only assistance while those users lack verification skills. Legg and colleagues warn that education can burden unrepresented people with learning both AI and law without replacing legal help. Proposed responses include accessible authoritative sources, targeted judicial inquiries, supervised navigation tools and alternative routes for users who opt out. Reported small-claims projects, readability uses and chatbot proposals demonstrate experimentation, not established improvements in dispute outcomes.

qs.q: However, the use of GenAI in small claims involves a rather different risk profile from its utilisation by lawyers and judges.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

qs.q: They may be the only source of advice or assistance some litigants receive.
qs.a: Artificial Intelligence (AI): Guidance for Judicial Office Holders (31 October 2025 refresh) · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an:
The selected academia and research sources broadly accept the proposition’s core: generative AI may assist legal and judicial work, but responsibility must remain with human professionals and verification must involve substantive professional judgment. They commonly ground this stance in persistent fabrication risks, documented filing failures, confidentiality and evidentiary-integrity concerns, and the danger that overreliance displaces independent legal analysis. They also reinforce the proposition’s descriptive account that courts use materially different verification-only, disclosure, certification and prohibition regimes.

As a professional voice, however, these curated sources materially develop the proposition rather than merely endorse it. The strongest extension is a governance framework combining practical education, organisational supervision, certification, calibrated sanctions and selective restrictions, with safeguards tailored to the cause and context of misuse. Other contributions identify verification drift under time and resource pressure, question whether checking costs erode claimed efficiency gains, distinguish professional expert-supervised use from consumer-facing access-to-justice applications, and extend accountability questions to courts’ own use of AI.

There is material internal variation. One strand argues that existing professional-conduct and procedural rules are sufficient and that AI-specific disclosure or broad bans are overinclusive, difficult to define and potentially conducive to covert use. Another favours certification and targeted prohibitions—particularly for witness evidence and expert reports—because they can make breaches easier to establish and protect evidentiary integrity. Some sources remain descriptive rather than normative, documenting divergent rules without choosing among them; several adoption, deterrence and access-to-justice claims are explicitly predictions or possibilities rather than demonstrated outcomes. One fragmentary source is insufficient to determine a position. These differences concern how accountability should be implemented, not whether AI authorship transfers responsibility or excuses defective work.

qs.q: Each of the solutions has a role to play and they are generally mutually reinforcing.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: Across this curated set, regulators, courts and professional bodies accept the proposition’s core: AI may assist legal and judicial work, but it does not assume professional or judicial responsibility, and its output requires substantive human verification before reliance. Their common reasons are generative AI’s capacity for plausible fabrication, outdated or jurisdictionally inapplicable law, incomplete analysis, bias and insecure handling of confidential information. These sources materially develop the proposition by translating that principle into operational controls: approved tools and training, authoritative-source checking, supervision and audit trails, restrictions on sensitive inputs, special treatment of witness and expert evidence, and prohibitions on autonomous court-facing action by agentic AI. Material internal variation concerns the mechanism rather than the accountability principle. Singapore, New Zealand, England and Wales, and Victoria’s 2026 note generally avoid routine disclosure but require users to explain AI use when asked; Canada’s Federal Court requires declarations for AI co-authorship; individual US judges impose certification or identification requirements; and some courts prohibit particular drafting uses. NSW applies especially strong controls to witness evidence and expert reports, while Singapore permits a safeguarded first draft but prohibits fabrication or alteration of evidence. Fifth Circuit commenters accept verification and responsibility but argue that broad AI-specific certification can be unclear, stigmatizing and redundant. Separate sources redirect attention toward court administration, data-transfer notice and user opt-outs, while the supplied New Jersey excerpt is too limited to establish a substantive position. These materials are chiefly normative guidance, rules and risk warnings; sanctions incidents illustrate the need for safeguards but do not establish general model error rates or prove that the safeguards work.

qs.q: Some courts have issued standing orders or local rules prohibiting the use of generative AI to draft legal filings or at least requiring certain forms of disclosure; others have declined to issue any such rules at all.
qs.a: Texas Professional Ethics Committee Opinion 705: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: This curated frontline-practitioner thread supports the proposition’s core: AI may assist legal work, but existing professional responsibility remains with the human user and output requires knowledgeable, substantive review before reliance. The quoted Australian court guidance also aligns with the synthesis’s jurisdiction-specific account of disclosure, requiring transparency in some circumstances or when the court requests it rather than imposing universal disclosure. Internal variation is material but does not reverse that position: one anonymous poster offers anecdotal concerns about poor AI-assisted work; another recognises potential time savings subject to competent review; separate posters defend willingness-to-pay pricing and predict major job and fee reductions. Those pricing and labour claims are ancillary—the job-loss forecast is unsupported—and do not challenge conditional use or human verification. Because the thread combines quoted judicial guidance with several anonymous contributors, it should not be treated as a unified practitioner view or as representative of frontline practitioners generally.

qs.q: This requires users of Generative AI to be guided by, and act in accordance with, their existing legal and professional responsibilities.[3] It follows that there will be circumstances where it is inappropriate to use Generative AI at all or where users ought to be transparent about its use.
qs.a: Recently had a deeper look at the capability of an AI platform (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread) · Frontline practitioners · 2026

qs.q: I can see how time can be saved on the actual grunt work of duplicating and summarising text, but a human who knows what they are doing needs to review the output and make it fit for purpose.
qs.a: Recently had a deeper look at the capability of an AI platform (RollOnFriday discussion-board thread) · Frontline practitioners · 2026

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources accept and materially develop the cluster’s principal proposition. Their common foundation is a copilot model: generative AI may assist legal or judicial work, but competence, candour, confidentiality, supervision, independent judgment and responsibility remain human obligations. They consistently treat verification as substantive professional review rather than a check limited to whether citations exist, extending it to factual support, legal relevance, currency, jurisdictional applicability, bias and client interests. The main internal variation concerns how to operationalise that responsibility. New Zealand and Singapore generally reject routine disclosure while allowing courts to inquire; Canada’s Federal Court requires declarations for AI acting as a co-author; several US judges require certification, disclosure or records; and others prohibit AI drafting. Commenters and academic analysis challenge broad AI-specific rules as unclear, duplicative and potentially burdensome, whereas disclosure regimes invoke fairness and judicial integrity. Further material extensions include non-delegable judicial decision-making, heightened safeguards for evidence, patent-specific disclosure where human inventorship is deficient, risk-based task selection, organisational controls and the possible cost of verification. Some sources redirect attention toward court administration, user data and opt-out rights, and a few excerpts are too incomplete to classify, but these variations do not displace the period’s overall development of conditional, accountable use. Because this is a curated set, these recurring themes show relationships among the selected sources rather than prevalence across courts, bars or jurisdictions; most support is normative or incident-based rather than evidence that particular safeguards are effective.

qs.q: Although the ABA Model Rules were not written to address specific technologies, they are comprehensive enough to permit the responsible and ethical use of generative AI tools in legal practice.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI may assist legal and judicial work only while humans retain substantive responsibility, and they materially develop it into an adoption-at-scale governance model. Their common reasons are persistent fabrication and bias risks, the inability of AI to verify itself reliably, confidentiality and security exposure, and the danger that fluent output or time pressure will erode checking. Accordingly, they translate responsibility into operational controls: authoritative-source verification, approved tools, training, supervision, data-handling restrictions, audit records and leadership accountability. Material variation concerns the intensity and location of those controls rather than the core proposition. England and Wales generally favours context-dependent disclosure and secondary assistance; NSW imposes certification, evidentiary prohibitions and prior leave for expert-report content; other guidance supports disclosure of AI-assisted judicial drafting, while some commentary predicts restrictions may drive use underground. Consumer-facing and self-represented-litigant applications also expose a limitation in the dominant model because expert verification may be unavailable. Adoption and benefit claims remain unevenly evidenced: surveys, reported use cases and institutional projects show experimentation and expectations, while litigation incidents illustrate risks without establishing general error rates or proving that particular safeguards work.

qs.q: Those who use artificial intelligence to conduct legal research notwithstanding these            risks have a professional duty therefore to check the accuracy of such research by            reference to authoritative sources, before using it in the course of their professional            work (to advise clients or before a court, for example).
qs.a: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank — Divisional Court Judgment on AI Hallucinations and the Hamid Jurisdiction · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Each of the solutions has a role to play and they are generally mutually reinforcing.
qs.a: The Promise and the Peril of the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Litigation · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the synthesis’s principal proposition: AI may assist legal and court work, but it does not transfer professional or judicial responsibility, and relied-upon output requires meaningful human verification. They build materially on that proposition by adapting it to newer and more operational settings—especially agentic AI, risk-proportionate oversight, organisational policies, traceability, confidentiality controls, evidence preparation and judicial communication. Common reasons are the risk of fabricated or inaccurate content, bias, loss of independent judgment, confidentiality breaches and harm to clients or the administration of justice. Material variation concerns implementation rather than the core principle: California bars autonomous court-facing action by agentic systems; Victoria and Singapore generally require users to be ready to identify AI assistance and explain verification if asked rather than mandating routine disclosure; Victoria imposes particular caution for evidence; and some sources focus more narrowly on overreliance, eDiscovery evidence standards or exploratory access-to-justice uses. The Verification-Value Paradox is more sceptical about whether safeguards preserve promised efficiencies, but still endorses substantive verification rather than rejecting conditional use. These normative rules, reported experiences and predictions do not establish either the effectiveness of the safeguards or general net benefits.

qs.q: Lawyers must not permit AI systems to autonomously file                      documents, communicate with the court, or make representations on                      the lawyer’s behalf.
qs.a: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: 7.6 Court users must be prepared to identify the specific portions of Court documents which were produced using AI and be able to explain how the output was verified.
qs.a: Practice Note SC Gen 25 — The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Court Users · Regulators & courts · 2026
